articles.title: Ukraine hit a data center operated by the Russian tech giant Yandex. How vulnerable is Russia’s internet to further drone attacks?
articles.body:
Ukraine hit a data center operated by the Russian tech giant Yandex. How vulnerable is Russia’s internet to further drone attacks?
What happened?
Overnight on October 8, Ukrainian forces struck Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, in Russia’s Ryazan region, with drones, causing a fire. No one was injured, but the data center temporarily shut down completely. This disrupted some of Yandex’s own services, as well as those of companies that used the tech giant’s infrastructure in Sasovo.
In the morning, users complained of problems accessing Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents. Disruptions then spread to Yandex Mail, the Yandex-owned Cian, Avito, IVI, MegaFon, Russian Railways, T-Bank, and several property developers and media outlets. The cascading disruptions across the Russian internet throughout the day may have been linked to an attempt to redistribute server capacity after the fire in Sasovo.
The data center occupies part of the former Sasta machine tool factory and houses two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, Lyapunov and Chervonenkis, which are used to train neural networks.
Whether these systems were damaged is not yet known. The overall extent of the damage is also unclear. Yandex shares have already fallen by more than 3% following the attack, according to Moscow Exchange data.
So it got hit. They’ll fix it, right?
We don’t know. Much depends on how badly the fire damaged the equipment. Even if restoring the data center is technically possible, it might simply not make sense, partly because of the threat of further attacks. After a series of successful Ukrainian strikes on large Wildberries warehouses, for example, the online retailer’s management decided to spread its inventory across smaller facilities. Yandex may take the same approach.
Some of the data stored at the Ryazan data center, however, may be recoverable. If Yandex customers uploaded their data to the cloud, those files were stored simultaneously at different company data centers — more precisely, in four “availability zones.” Yandex said in 2019:
All of this data is replicated: When an object is edited, created, or deleted, every copy is updated.
Things are a little more complicated for other companies’ virtual machines hosted there. Customers are responsible for backing up that data themselves. They could have used the separate paid service Yandex Cloud Backup, which would also have stored their data at several data centers. Or they could have chosen another solution — or made no backups at all.
Why do services stop working when data centers are hit?
Because these facilities store user data and house the servers that companies and organizations rent to run their websites or internal infrastructure.
Data centers can withstand a temporary power outage thanks to their own diesel generators, the loss of an individual communications link thanks to connections to multiple telecom providers, and even a small fire thanks to automatic fire suppression systems. But, like online retailers’ warehouses, they have proved defenseless against drone strikes. Unless, of course, they are housed in former Cold War shelters — Europe has several such data centers.
Should we expect more attacks like these — as with oil refineries, Wildberries, and Ozon?
Nothing can be predicted with certainty during a war. But the context matters.
The strike on Yandex’s data center looks like a logical Ukrainian response to systematic Russian military attacks on Ukrainian digital hubs, including Cosmonova and Datagroup facilities. Since late September, Russian forces have damaged or destroyed the data centers of at least eight companies.
Russia’s Defense Ministry officially called these strikes a “forced digital detox.” Today, a few hours after the attack on Yandex’s data center, Andriy Kovalenko, the former head of the Center for Countering Disinformation at Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, wrote:
Two can play that game.
Which other data centers in Russia could be targeted? And could strikes on them bring down the entire Russian internet?
Any technology hub could be at risk, but a nationwide digital blackout is unlikely.
Sarkis Darbinyan, a lawyer specializing in digital rights and an expert with RKS.global, told Meduza that a single strike on a regional data center cannot take down a major service entirely. Modern IT companies have infrastructure spread across the country, so when equipment fails, user traffic is automatically rerouted to backup systems. Russia’s main data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region and are very well protected. Disabling them all would be an extremely ambitious undertaking, Darbinyan said. Russia has close to 200 data centers in total.
Darbinyan believes further targeted attacks on regional facilities belonging to Rostelecom, Sber, VK, or Selectel are possible in theory:
They could cause local disruptions, but would affect local residents more than the country as a whole: Regional government systems, online school gradebooks, medical customer relationship management systems, and internet-connected cash registers would temporarily stop working. These services could be down for anywhere from a few hours to a day while administrators reconfigure the systems.
Another potential target for Ukrainian forces is MSK-IX, Russia’s largest internet exchange point. It has become a “symbol of the centralization of the Russian internet,” Darbinyan said. If MSK-IX is hit, he told Meduza, internet access across the country could slow dramatically, alternative communications links could become overloaded, and the websites of small companies and local providers could temporarily become inaccessible. Even then, however, the internet would not shut down entirely, Darbinyan said:
This is a fundamental feature of the network, built into it back in the days of ARPANET so that it could withstand even a nuclear strike. So attacks like these only impair services temporarily, for a few hours — they certainly don’t cause a complete digital collapse.
Are these strikes legal? And why attack internet infrastructure at all? After all, it’s civilians, not the military, who suffer the most…
Indeed, if we accept that this is primarily civilian infrastructure, neither army’s strikes on data centers appear justified. The Geneva Conventions explicitly state that a facility is a military objective if it makes an “effective contribution to military action” and its neutralization “offers a definite military advantage” to the attacking side. In cases of doubt, it is presumed to be civilian — meaning this infrastructure cannot be attacked without clear evidence.
Unfortunately, when it comes to data centers, Russian forces — and, following their lead, Ukrainian forces — are clearly ignoring the question of legality. For example, Russia’s Defense Ministry justified its strikes on Ukrainian data centers by saying that the grounds of one facility “were used by units of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry and other security agencies to store dual-use goods.” Another data center allegedly handled “the processing and transmission of intelligence for the Ukrainian armed forces.” The ministry provided no evidence for these claims.
As for the military rationale, at least some data centers meet the criteria for targets in long-range strike campaigns. Meduza’s Explainers desk previously set out these criteria:
- The facilities are poorly protected and can be destroyed with just a few drones carrying small warheads
- Their coordinates are well known
- They contain large quantities of valuable goods
- Systematically destroying these businesses can damage the enemy’s economy
- Disrupting internet infrastructure can also make civilians feel just how much the war is costing their country and, in theory, fuel public discontent with the government’s actions.

articles.title: Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant
articles.body:
A drone attack overnight on 8 October caused a fire that hit part of Yandex's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, about 580 km from Ukraine, and the site is fully stopped, the Russian tech company told Russian media. The data center sits on the grounds of Sasta, a sanctioned machine-tool plant, Russian outlet Astra said, citing Wikimapia data. Astra's OSINT analyst found from eyewitness footage that the fire hit the plant.
Since late September, Russia has been striking data centers in Kyiv that keep Ukraine's internet and online services running. Now a drone attack has stopped one of the data centers that Russia's largest tech company relies on.
Yandex counts the damage
Yandex warned that some services may be unavailable, while its core services kept running and no one was hurt. Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov claimed two drones were downed, a roof caught fire at an enterprise in the Sasovo district, and windows were blown out in several homes.
The power failure took down a wide range of Yandex Cloud infrastructure, including computing capacity, networks, data storage, databases, Kubernetes, cloud services, AI, and security and monitoring systems, Ukrainian outlet ZN.ua reported, citing Exilenova+.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the plant was hit, without naming an attacker. The channel said Sasta, which claims a place on Russia's register of defense-industry companies, makes computer-controlled machine tools, including five-axis machining centers, and previously supplied the Tactical Missiles Corporation (KTRV) and Roscosmos. The plant's value to the arms industry lies in machines that cut precision parts, not in finished weapons, the channel said.
Citing Exilenova+, Militarnyi reported that Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the plant. It also linked Sasta to Iskander missile supply chains. No source has said whether the plant or the data center was the target, and no Ukrainian official has claimed the Sasovo strike. Sasta has been under US sanctions since November 2023, UK sanctions since February 2024, and Ukrainian sanctions since April 2025, a sanctions database shows.
Salavat: Kyiv reports a hit
Ukrainian forces hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat complex in Bashkortostan, about 1,380 km from the front line, causing a fire, Ukraine's General Staff said. It said the complex processes up to 10 million metric tons of hydrocarbons a year and serves Russia's armed forces. Its key unit, the ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil refining unit launched in 2012, can process 6 million metric tons a year, Militarnyi reported. Astra's analyst placed the fire a few kilometers outside Salavat, possibly near the refinery.
Salavat Mayor Marat Zagidullin claimed that debris from several drones fell in the industrial zone that morning and started a fire.
"The enterprise continues to work," he said.
Astra noted earlier hits on the complex on 24 September 2025, on 14 July 2026, when refining fully stopped, and on 13 August 2026.
Russia's strikes on Ukraine's data centers
Russia has repeatedly hit data centers in Kyiv since 23 September. Strikes hit the COSMONOVA data center twice, the second time knocking it out, and the Parkovyi data center stopped working completely on 1 October after a series of strikes. In early October, Russia destroyed the dline.ua data center in Kyiv.

articles.title: Kremlin-linked Matryoshka bots accuse France’s Macron of militarism and Germany’s Merz of profiting from aid to Ukraine
articles.body:
The Kremlin-linked Matryoshka bot network has launched a new wave of disinformation targeting European leaders, this time focusing on French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The campaign is highlighted by contradicting false claims that Macron is both overly militaristic and dangerously weak, along with false accusations that Merz has personally profited from aid intended for Ukraine. The posts were collected by AntiBot4Navalny, a project that monitors bot activity on social media.
Macron’s “toxic masculinity”
One of the main themes promoted by the Matryoshka network was France’s test of a new ballistic missile, which was indeed launched from a nuclear-powered submarine on Oct. 6 with Macron looking on. In a post on X, the French president wrote:
“Very few nations possess such expertise…To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful.”
In videos circulated by the bot network, Macron is accused of “toxic masculinity.” The claim is falsely attributed to Kimberly Kagan, president of the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), an organization whose brand, logo, and personnel are frequently used by the Matryoshka network to lend credence to its false claims. Kagan is also made to appear to say that such weapons would be incapable of standing up to Russia.
Another video, falsely presented as coming from French broadcaster RFI, says Macron is bluffing and claims France’s military sector is “catastrophically” behind “the rest of the world,” leaving him with nothing to do but “wave around cardboard missiles that cannot even get out of the water.”
Another video, falsely attributed to the media monitoring company NewsGuard, claims the footage of the missile test itself was generated using artificial intelligence.
Some of the posts also link the missile test to protests by high school students that spread across France over the past week. The bot network claims the students are protesting the country’s militarization; however, the demonstrations were actually driven by problems in the education system, including concerns over teacher shortages, substandard facilities, and the overall quality of instruction.
The videos also claim that some French politicians fled the country because of the protests, withdrawing from the presidential race. Speaking in the name of a supposed French analyst, Matryoshka claims that the demonstrations “showed the true face of French politicians” and that Macron himself is “a worthless person.”
Merz’s ratings and alleged corruption schemes
Matryoshka also targeted neighboring Germany. According to the bot network’s claims, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is at the center of a corruption scandal. Videos falsely presented as coming from outlets including Bellingcat allege that Merz pockets at least 25% of every aid tranche sent to Ukraine.
Earlier this week, Merz announced a new major aid package for Kyiv worth 1 billion euros. In one Matryoshka video, Bellingcat founder Eliot Higgins is falsely depicted as saying Merz would personally receive at least 250 million euros from the tranche, while Ukrainian officials would allegedly divide most of the remainder among themselves. The fake Bellingcat content claims similar schemes operate in other countries and says Macron’s income has “tripled” thanks to a similar arrangement.
Following the real news about the 1 billion-euro aid package, other Matryoshka fake posts focused on an alleged drop in Merz’s approval rating, claiming it had fallen 23%. The bots also claim that the protests in France will soon spread to Germany, citing the country’s large migrant population as the supposed trigger while predicting an escalation in clashes with police within the next six months.
AntiBot4Navalny said such posts may offer clues about issues currently concerning the Kremlin, as bot networks can serve as an indicator of what topics the Kremlin is interested in amplifying.
What is Matryoshka?
Antibot4Navalny’s researchers coined the name Matryoshka to describe a Russian operation that produces and spreads fake stories through a coordinated infrastructure of bots, trolls, and anonymous platforms. Its aim is to create artificial information “noise” and manipulate perceptions of events both inside Russia and abroad. The Antibot4Navalny project named the operation after the eponymous Russian nesting doll — the bots hide behind one another, and disinformation is spread in layers across different platforms, making the source harder to identify.
The mechanism works in two ways. First, it creates large numbers of fake profiles posing as ordinary people, independent media outlets, or think tanks. These accounts generate dozens of posts a day, imitating local styles of speech. Second, identical content is launched simultaneously across multiple social media platforms at the same time. In order to appear convincing, the bots use the logos of well-known Western media outlets and human rights groups.

articles.title: 22 killed in Russian missile strike on Pryluky, including five children
articles.body:
The death toll from Russia's 7 October missile strike on Pryluky, a city in Chernihiv Oblast in northern Ukraine, has risen to 22, including five children, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on 8 October. Another 54 people were injured, and 15 were rescued from the rubble.
Pryluky suffered the heaviest losses in Russia's 7 October attack, which struck cities across Ukraine. The attack involved about 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, as well as Shahed drones.
Search ends with 15 rescued
Seven of the injured are children, and the rescued include a 5-year-old. The search-and-rescue operation, which involved more than 500 emergency workers, has ended, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
A five-story building hit early in the morning
Russia attacked Pryluky with cruise missiles and directly hit a five-story apartment building, Chernihiv Oblast head Viacheslav Chaus said. The strike came in the morning, when people were still asleep.
The strike hit the apartment building, a children's and youth creativity center, and a business, according to the National Police.
The death toll rose through 7 October and overnight. On the morning of 7 October, the National Police reported five dead and 26 injured. By the afternoon, the State Emergency Service put the figure at 14, including four children. By the morning of 8 October, it had reached 22, Chaus said. Four of the children died at the scene, and one died in hospital.
Russian strikes in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia
Russia attacked Kyiv and 12 oblasts overnight on 7 October, Zelenskyy said. Two people were killed in each of Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia.
Air defense downed or suppressed five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 drones, while missiles and drones hit 18 locations, according to the Air Force.

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi airports after ‘final warning’ (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Houthis strike Saudi airports after ‘final warning’ (VIDEOS)
Yemen’s Houthi forces have reportedly struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with missiles for the second time in a day, hours after issuing a “final warning” to airlines against operating in Saudi airspace.
The Houthis hit the airport with two cruise missiles on Thursday evening, the group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree announced in a statement. Houthi forces also hit Abha Airport and King Khalid Air Base with ballistic missiles, Saree added.
“The strikes were precise and direct, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the two airports and causing damage to them and the air base,” Saree said. The Saudi government has not acknowledged the strikes. The head of the Saudi military coalition against the Houthis in Yemen, Turki al-Maliki, has claimed that two missiles were intercepted before they reached Riyadh, and one was intercepted before it reached King Khalid Air Base.
Earlier on Thursday, Houthi forces hit King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile, which Saree said “struck its target with precision and caused the disruption of airport operations.”
Video footage shared by the Houthis showed a thick plume of smoke rising from the apron of the airport, while footage shared on social media suggested that the missile landed directly on a parked aircraft belonging to the Saudia airline.
After the first strike, Saree issued what he called a “final warning to all global airlines,” warning them to stay out of Saudi airspace, “which has become a theater for our military operations.”
Around 40% of flights in and out of Riyadh were canceled on Thursday. Almost two dozen carriers have canceled or suspended service to the Saudi capital amid the Kingdom’s escalating conflict with the Houthis. Air India and Lufthansa both announced on Thursday that they would not fly into Riyadh until next week.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Fighting resumed this July after Saudi-backed forces struck the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen.
The conflict escalated further in September, when the Houthis made their largest territorial gains in years, taking Mocha and key positions along the Red Sea coast and around Bab el-Mandeb.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment
articles.body:
- The death toll from Russia’s latest attack on Ukraine has climbed to 28, its interior minister, Ivan Vyhivskyi, has said. Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones on Wednesday. The heaviest losses were in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-storey residential building. Twenty people died in the attack, including five children, said Pryluky’s regional governor, Vyacheslav Chaus. On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb of the capital.
- In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and as they worked their way down brought out 15 survivors. About 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said.
- Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the Pryluky attack one of Russia’s “most vile”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian president said. “This was one of the most vile strikes.”
- Russia’s defence ministry has said its forces struck a vessel heading to the Ukrainian Black seaport of Odesa with cargo for the Ukrainian military. The statement on Telegram on Wednesday gave no further details of the strike. The ministry also said Russian drones had hit infrastructure in Ukrainian ports, without elaborating.
- Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for worsening security in the Black Sea on Wednesday. Early on Tuesday, two ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone, with one sinking and the other damaged. The crew of the damaged ship were rescued but the crew of the sunken one remain missing. Yotova did not directly blame Russia, but said on Wednesday that the war had led to “a significant deterioration” in security for commercial vessels in the region. Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing crew.
- European Union envoys approved 1,646 new designations under the bloc’s sanctions regime for Russia, with most focused on the country’s military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said on Wednesday. More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the chain of production of Russia’s ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko advises residents with friends or family outside the city to consider leaving temporarily amid escalating Russian attacks
articles.body:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko advises residents with friends or family outside the city to consider leaving temporarily amid escalating Russian attacks
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has suggested that residents with friends or relatives outside the Ukrainian capital consider leaving the city temporarily, he told AFP in an interview.
“Every day brings new reports of destroyed buildings, of people injured and killed, as the shelling of our city intensifies,” the mayor said. “Today the issue is survival,” he added.
He stressed that he would never call for a full evacuation of the city.
“That’s Putin’s goal… the best scenario for Putin is that we all leave and hand over our empty cities and our country to him,” Klitschko said.
Klitschko also said Kyiv is preparing backup heating systems for winter and stockpiling fuel, food, and drinking water. But he said even proper preparations might not be enough if air defenses cannot repel the attacks.
Russia began stepping up its attacks on Kyiv in September. Daily attacks from September 22 to 28 alone killed 13 Kyiv residents and injured more than 160. In early October, Russian forces also began striking some of Kyiv’s most important transport links — the bridges across the Dnipro River, which had not previously come under attack. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military commanders to disregard the rules of warfare when carrying out airstrikes on Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky has a message for Washington: Don’t call peace impossible while refusing to put more pressure on Putin
articles.body:
Zelensky has a message for Washington: Don’t call peace impossible while refusing to put more pressure on Putin
Meduza presents statements about the war in Ukraine by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in an October 8 interview with the Greek newspaper Kathimerini, as well as the response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Marco Rubio
Well, unfortunately, [Russia’s invasion of Ukraine] seems to be going into its fifth year, which was never the original plan. I don’t think that was Putin’s plan for this war, so it hasn’t gone the way he planned it. And I think what it is now, unfortunately, is a strategic stalemate, which is a dangerous thing. Strategic stalemates are only broken in one of two ways: (a) through a negotiated settlement, or (b) through escalation by one side or both that ends up spreading beyond the confines of the original conflict.
Right now, there don’t seem to be prospects of a negotiated settlement. We are prepared to play whatever role we can in making that happen. And we have tried in the past, but so far it’s been elusive. The Russians have defined victory as the totality of Donetsk; they’ve repeatedly stated that as their goal, and they continue to state that as their goal. And that’s a condition that, for Ukraine, is simply unacceptable. And so, a diplomatic solution has eluded us, but we are prepared, if we can play a constructive role, to make it happen.
In the meantime, we watch with great concern as escalation could happen. Just yesterday, some ships were attacked in the Black Sea through a coordinated drone attack. We’re worried about a sabotage operation in a neighboring country that can spiral out of control. And, obviously, I think there are clear indications that Russia will use the upcoming winter as something they want to use to destroy what remains of the electric grid in Ukraine and force them into capitulation.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown more effective in its ability to conduct long-range strikes deep into Russia. So, we share the same concern. The whole world is going about this thing like something that could escalate and perhaps become a broader conflict. So, we stand prepared to facilitate and continue to explore any opportunity for a negotiated settlement. We think it would be good for Russia and Ukraine, but so far, it’s proving elusive.
Volodymyr Zelensky
We’ve heard all sorts of things during this war. So many dead ends, difficult situations, and so on. We — ordinary people, leaders, politicians — back ourselves into corners. Even on the first day of the war, we weren’t cornered, because one man tried to back an entire nation into a dead end, and the people rose up and defended their country. We didn’t let the Russians do that. We had high hopes that we would receive support. And that support began to arrive.
But after that, you can’t, you see, on the one hand make deals with the Russians about some future economic projects and, on the other, say that we’re in some kind of political situation, a diplomatic dead end, or whatever. We’re not at a diplomatic dead end. Cut off his economy entirely. Sew Russia’s mouth shut. Stop feeding them with your sales. Just impose sanctions on their weapons.
Make Starlink available to us, to Ukraine. You made it available when you were responding to Iran, and everything worked there. Israel had complete control of the skies. Complete control of the skies over Iran. So when you need it, it works that way.
Right now, we’re talking to various colleagues in Europe and America, and I tell them frankly: China is developing an alternative to Starlink. And they’re getting close. And they’ll give it to Russia. Russia could gain that kind of dominance. We’re talking to Europeans who are also developing several technologies along these lines. They’d be happy to help us, but they’re still not as close to achieving the result we need.
And simply controlling the skies so we can defend ourselves — we’re talking about defense here. The United States has that capability. It does. It would cost them nothing, absolutely nothing, to help Ukraine. And I’ve said frankly: Give us that. Help us defend our airspace and dominate it. Then Putin will come to the negotiating table. Why? Because he’ll lose everything. He’ll lose everything. Three months, two months — he’ll lose everything.
But instead, we’re waiting for the Chinese to develop their equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where’s the truth in that? Where’s the honesty? Where is any of it? What dead end? What dead end? This isn’t a dead end. It’s called unwillingness. It’s not a dead end.

articles.title: Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
articles.body:
Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
India was the world’s second-largest arms importer in 2025, partly aided by a historically large naval buildout, according to a Russian think tank that tracks weapons purchases and military expenditures.
The South Asian nuclear power has been rapidly building up its armed forces following a brief clash with neighbor Pakistan last year, triggered by a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir.
India’s identified military imports were worth $6.97 billion, or 5.83% of the global total, and the country is projected to retain the position through 2029, the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT) said.
Poland came in first with $11.91 billion, while Australia was narrowly behind India at $6.96 billion.
Among the major Indian deliveries cited by CAWAT was the Russian-built frigate Tamal, which joined the Indian Navy in July 2025. Two more Project 11356 frigates are being built at India’s Goa Shipyard with assistance from Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport. 
India also commissioned the Vaghsheer, the sixth and final Kalvari-class submarine built by state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders under license from France’s Naval Group. The six-submarine program was valued at $3.6 billion, according to CAWAT.
The Indian Navy is undergoing its largest expansion in history, with plans to induct or commission 18 warships this year. 
New Delhi imported $25.44 billion worth of arms in the 2022-2025 period, placing it third behind Saudi Arabia and Qatar in CAWAT’s four-year rankings. Its annual imports rose from $3.87 billion in 2024 to $6.97 billion last year. 
The think tank projects India’s arms imports at $45.65 billion over 2026-2029, keeping the country in the second position. Poland is expected to remain at the top with $55.32 billion worth of imports, followed by Germany at $36.48 billion. The forecast is based on existing contracts, officially announced procurement plans, and expected tenders as of December 2025. 
Poland’s rise has been particularly sharp. Its arms imports climbed from $2.17 billion in 2022 to $11.91 billion in 2025, driven by major purchases including US-made Abrams tanks and South Korean K2 tanks.
CAWAT projects global arms imports at almost $633 billion over the 2026-2029 period, up 52.5% from in the preceding four years. The center expects Europe to take a larger share of global demand during the period.
The ranking covers identified commercial arms deliveries and does not include weapons supplied free of charge, including Western military aid to Ukraine.
CAWAT’s methodology differs from that of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), which measures the volume of major weapons transfers using a trend-indicator value rather than their sale price. SIPRI says its figures should not be directly compared with the financial value of arms transfers.

articles.title: NATO attempts to cool tensions with Russia ahead of key nuclear exercise
articles.body:
Crew members of aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman are pictured during a NATO vigilance activity in the Mediterranean on May 23, 2022. | Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that an upcoming nuclear drill in Italy is nothing to fear, with tensions high between the alliance and Moscow.
NATO announced Thursday that 17 allies will participate in the annual Steadfast Noon exercise from Oct. 13-23. But this year, the exercise follows a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after allies conducted exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave in August.
“We have been doing this every year and … this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry,” said Nassima Barrows, NATO’s nuclear policy director. “This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate.”
Advertisement
“Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability,” she told reporters.
Following the previous NATO exercises, Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening to hit allied territory and mentioning the use of its nuclear arsenal — a move that NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte publicly rebuked last week.
Tensions are rising as European countries accuse Russia of sabotage and growing so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
“Our intention is to really keep things calm,” said a senior NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Russian officials “keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood.”
U.S. Col. David Bull, chief of NATO’s nuclear operations, said the exercise has garnered “similar” participation to previous years and involves everything from a “simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise” — but “no live nuclear weapons.”
It will also feature dual-capable aircraft and ground troops to support the exercise and train on loading, fueling, and maintaining planes, a senior NATO military official added.
Russia’s embassy to Belgium didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm
articles.body:
The growing popularity of far-right parties across Europe is sparking worries in NATO that they could weaken public support for rearmament and military aid to Ukraine as risks grow of a confrontation with Russia.
In France, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Poland and Romania, these parties are looking to turn voters’ cost-of-living concerns into opposition to aid for Kyiv, and rejection of higher national defense budgets and a greater role for the EU in defense — although each party has often sharply diverging views on those issues.
France’s National Rally leader Marine Le Pen last month called for limiting aid to Ukraine, saying: “financially, we can’t do it anymore.”
Advertisement
Roberto Vannacci, a former general and MEP who leads the far-right National Future party, which is increasingly challenging Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, called for a rethink of defense spending. “Let’s evaluate whether this military spending is justified: in my opinion, it isn’t, especially at a time when commodity prices are hitting record highs,” he said last week.
The challenge for Europe’s mainstream parties is how to sustain support for higher defense budgets even if that means competing with welfare and other priorities.
“People are struggling with the rising cost of living across the board … so there’s room for populistic rhetoric about how much should we support Ukraine financially, or how much should we invest in defense,” said Janne Kuusela, permanent secretary at Finland’s defense ministry.
The dilemma is sharpening as several large NATO members, including France, Italy and Poland, face elections in 2027, when far-right parties stand a real chance of coming to power. Many countries are also beginning talks on next year’s budgets.
For NATO, a spending slowdown would complicate efforts to meet the alliance’s target of spending 5% of GDP on defense and security by 2035. Four NATO diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely, said the risk is a growing concern, though some said its effects may not be clear until next year’s budget cycle.
“We’re already in a situation where we need to catch up” with Russia, said a NATO military official. “So far, we’re on a positive trajectory — if someone closes the faucet, there’s a risk of losing capabilities.”
Advertisement
Turning the tide
European countries and Canada are expected to spend $634 billion on core defense needs this year, an 11% hike relative to 2025. But public support has limits.
In eight European countries, an average of 46.2% of respondents said they would not back higher defense spending if it meant higher taxes, while 35.5% were in favor, according to an August poll assessed by the European Council on Foreign Relations and shared with POLITICO. More people were opposed to increasing taxes to finance military spending in Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Respondents in the Netherlands, Sweden and the U.K. were more likely to accept higher taxes for military spending.
Protests against higher defense spending have taken place in Rome, Brussels and Madrid this year, with demonstrators criticizing cuts to funding for hospitals, universities and social services.
A damaged residential building is seen in Kyiv after a Russian missile strike on July 6, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images
Support for Ukraine is declining as well, according to NATO’s internal polling from this spring, falling from 59% in 2025 to 55% this year, with lethal aid the least popular form of support.
Far-right pushback on defense varies across Europe and falls broadly into three categories: opposition to military aid for Ukraine; rejection of EU-level defense projects; and criticism of defense spending more broadly. Yet all threaten to halt the continent’s effort to rearm rapidly and jointly — and limit Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
The right’s political foes warn that opposition plays into the Kremlin’s hands. “The pressure from the right doesn’t actually come from the right, but largely from Moscow,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said. Parties such as National Rally and the AfD have longstanding ties with Russia, though they have sought to shake off their links in recent years.
Defense spending pressure
The political risk varies by country. Le Pen is a front-runner to become French president, while the AfD has made gains at the regional level but is unlikely to take national office soon.
Far-right gains are putting centrist parties under pressure to defend higher spending or consider cuts to retain public support.
“There is a risk that the formally pro-European mainstream across Europe might be too timid to spend … as would be necessary on defence,” said Paweł Zerka, senior policy fellow at the ECFR.
While Le Pen’s National Rally has indicated that she would respect France’s current trajectory of increasing military spending, Italy’s Meloni last week proposed spending €8 billion less on defense than the government’s initial proposal amid pressure from her far-right coalition partner, the League.
“You can’t spend on weapons what you can’t spend on pensions, excise tax relief, or utility bills,” Claudio Borghi, a League senator, said last week.
Advertisement
In Poland, President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the right-wing Law and Justice party, tried but failed to block access to nearly €44 billion in EU SAFE defense loans, saying the scheme risked making Poland dependent on Brussels and saddling future generations with debt.
Pressure to rethink defense spending could make it harder for NATO members to fund the capabilities officials say are needed to deter Russia, as capitals begin talks this month on determining the alliance’s war plans, which are due by 2029.
A slowdown by larger members such as France and Italy would have broader effects because they account for a greater share of defense investment and aid to Kyiv, one of the NATO diplomats said.
“If bigger countries stop making progress, then NATO will stop making progress,” the diplomat said. “You weaken NATO, you weaken Europe’s ability to defend itself, and you make Ukraine … more vulnerable.”
It could also affect the sum earmarked for defense in the EU’s next long-term budget if talks stretch on into next year, said Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow and defense economics analyst at the Bruegel think tank.
“Nationalists are all only interested in their country, they don’t want to work together with other European countries,” said German lawmaker Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee.

articles.title: Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization
articles.body:
Lithuania plans to deploy up to 100 soldiers to support border guards along its frontier with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said on 7 October.
Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has described the deployment as a preventive measure linked to possible Russian mobilization and a recent incident on the Latvia-Belarus border, where masked, armed escorts tried to push a group of migrants into Latvia. Katelynas said Lithuania could face people trying to avoid mobilization and seeking asylum.
Kaunas said he had granted permission to use Lithuanian soldiers to strengthen border protection for the next several weeks.
“The order starts being implemented immediately,” he wrote on Facebook.
Russia denies a new mobilization
The Kremlin denies a new mobilization is coming. In early September, Russian President Vladimir Putin called reports of one "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence services say Russia's General Staff has prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027. On 28 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "in effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization."
Frontier-station patrols for a couple of weeks, possibly longer
On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. A company-sized unit was planned for the assignment, initially for two weeks, with the option to extend. Soldiers will patrol with border guards in frontier-station areas, while mobile patrols, mobile observation posts, and military police crews may be added as needed. The army described the deployment as preventive and a normal form of interagency cooperation.
Kaunas had told LRT TV the soldiers would stay until 16 October. On the morning of 8 October, he said the deployment "was supposed to start" overnight and that he would check with the army. On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. Kaunas also said that “on the Kaliningrad side” there were no physical barriers, unlike the border with Belarus.
Lithuania says its border guards are stretched
On 8 October, Katelynas said the border guard service’s capacity was insufficient, with shifts growing while officer numbers were not increasing. He said the threat level had not changed. In a Facebook post the previous day, he said the situation at Lithuania’s border was calm and there was no reason to panic. He said Russia was planning mobilization after the elections and that Lithuania may face people trying to avoid it and seeking asylum.
Lithuania's State Border Guard Service had turned back 1,693 people trying to cross illegally from Belarus this year and about 26,300 since the migration crisis began, as reported by ELTA on 8 October. Katelynas said 43 migrants tried to enter southern Lithuania last week and were turned back.

articles.title: Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter
articles.body:
Power outages have returned to Kyiv after Russian attacks damaged the energy infrastructure supplying the capital, with authorities warning that the situation could worsen as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine’s energy system ahead of winter.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power, heating, and other critical infrastructure to disrupt the systems civilians depend on and create a humanitarian crisis during winter. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that this winter will be especially severe, as Russia has expanded its strike capabilities since the summer and Ukraine continues to face shortages of air-defense systems needed to protect its energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo said on 8 October that emergency outages were being imposed in parts of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast because of falling voltage in the high-voltage network. Previously announced hourly schedules were suspended, with predictable schedules to resume once the system stabilizes.
In the evening, further disruption came after a Russian attack on an energy facility important to Kyiv. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said that energy workers were working to restore power.
Kyiv has been under Russian attack throughout the day, with four people killed and 19 injured.
The attack continues into the evening of 8 October, with air raid alerts active across most of the country.
Kyiv loses power, water, and public transport
The damage throughout the day quickly spread beyond electricity.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said power disruptions temporarily halted metro trains and escalators. Part of the capital’s public transport system was also suspended because of the lack of electricity.
Reduced power to water infrastructure caused lower pressure on the right bank of the Dnipro, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. Some buildings could temporarily lose water, the administration warned.
Russia is hitting the energy system as winter approaches
The outages come as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
Ukrenergo said Russian attacks had caused new power outages in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The company said damaged equipment was already limiting the grid’s ability to supply consumers and warned that further Russian strikes could rapidly change the situation.
For 9 October, Ukrenergo announced all-day power restrictions in affected regions, including hourly outages for some consumers. Industrial and business consumers will also face restrictions. The company urged Ukrainians to conserve electricity, particularly during the evening peak from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Ukraine’s energy authorities have been warning about the consequences of repeated Russian attacks for months. In late September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said attacks on energy facilities had been occurring almost daily since the summer, with the September 29–30 attack marking the first massive combined strike on the energy system since the previous heating season.
The renewed strikes mark the beginning of Russia’s winter campaign against the energy system, with Russian missiles and drones increasingly targeting power-generation and transmission infrastructure in Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Russia has openly threatened another winter of blackouts
The campaign follows years of Russian attacks aimed at disrupting the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainian homes heated and supplied with electricity and water during the winter.
In August, Russia’s Defense Ministry openly taunted Ukrainians over its attacks on energy-related infrastructure, posting images of attack drones with the message that Ukrainians would “get a freeze” in winter.
Russia’s strategy has repeatedly linked attacks on electricity infrastructure to disruptions in heating and water supplies. This makes damage to the power grid particularly consequential as temperatures fall: a strike on an electrical facility can leave not only homes without lights, but also affect water pumps, heating systems, transportation, and other essential services.
The return of blackouts to Kyiv before the heating season is fully underway is an early indication of the pressure Russia’s renewed energy campaign is putting on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
Ukrainian drone operators struck a Russian Osa short-range air defense system twice on the Donbas front, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of the 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems on October 8.
The video shows Ukrainian drones engaging the Russian surface-to-air missile system during a broader series of strikes against military equipment and logistics.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Signum operators highlighted the irony themselves, playing on the system’s name—Osa means “Wasp.”
“We ‘stung’ the Osa twice,” the battalion said.
The same footage shows Signum operators targeting Russian logistics across the Donbas, including pickup trucks, UAZ vans, cargo trucks, semitrailers, and other vehicles used to move troops, ammunition, and equipment.
The battalion said its crews routinely work against the routes Russian forces depend on to keep frontline units supplied, with the Osa becoming one of the more valuable targets caught during the latest operation.
The 9K33 Osa is a Soviet-designed mobile short-range air defense system developed beginning in 1960 and introduced into service in 1971. At the time, it was notable for combining its target-acquisition radar, tracking radar, and missiles on a single amphibious vehicle, allowing the system to operate without separate radar vehicles.
Built on the six-wheeled BAZ-5937 chassis, the Osa was designed to accompany ground forces and protect them from low-flying aircraft and other aerial threats. Its radar can detect targets at distances of roughly 30 kilometers, while later variants can engage targets at ranges of around 10 kilometers.
The system underwent several upgrades during its service life, including the Osa-AKM introduced in 1980, which brought improved tracking and enclosed missile canisters.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.

articles.title: Iran war could force Israel to postpone election, IDF chief tells US officials
articles.body:
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has told senior U.S. government and military officials that a renewed military escalation with Iran could force Israel to postpone its general election, currently scheduled for October 27, according to a source familiar with the discussions.
Zamir raised serious concerns about the security and political consequences of another direct confrontation with Tehran, warning that a major outbreak of fighting so close to the vote could make holding the election on schedule impossible. Israel’s security chiefs have already described the weeks leading up to Oct. 27 as a particularly sensitive period and held a joint assessment this week focused on ensuring the election can be held safely.
The warning comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that Washington would not attack Iran “at any time prior to the midterm elections” on November 3. Trump said talks with Tehran were “productive,” while insisting that the pressure campaign and blockade against Iran would remain in force.
Despite Trump’s declaration, the IDF remains on heightened alert. The Israeli Air Force and Military Intelligence Directorate are maintaining readiness for a possible escalation with Iran, which the military continues to regard as its primary strategic theater. Any Israeli involvement in another major confrontation with Tehran would be coordinated with Washington.
The IDF and U.S. military have remained in close coordination since the end of the latest round of fighting with Iran. Israeli military intelligence is meanwhile building an extensive new target bank inside Iran, covering ballistic missiles, launch and production infrastructure and sites connected to Tehran’s nuclear program. The IDF declined to comment on Zamir’s reported remarks.
The warning fits a broader pattern of heightened preparations ahead of the election. Zamir recently canceled a planned trip to the United States, where he had been due to meet the commander of U.S. Central Command and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, saying the security situation made it inappropriate for him to leave Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also warned during a visit to Tel Nof Air Base last week that there were “signs” Israel’s enemies could attempt an attack ahead of the election. “Don’t mess with us, not now and not ever,” he said. “Our long arm will reach you anywhere and at any time.”

articles.title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Is Aware of US-Russia Economic Discussions
articles.body:
Ukraine is aware of the content of various discussions between US and Russian authorities, but has no intentions of making the details public yet, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Zelensky made the remarks while speaking to reporters on Thursday, Oct. 8, in response to a question about which economic agreements Washington and Moscow are discussing.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We know a lot… about various dialogues, but I am simply not ready to talk about them publicly and in detail,” Zelensky said, according to Ukrinform.
Although the President did not specify which discussions he was referring to, his comments came hours after Reuters reported – citing five anonymous sources familiar with the matter, including a White House official – that US and Russia had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
Nord Stream reportedly discussed
According to Reuters, the talks involved senior US special envoy Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kushner reportedly sees business deals as key to securing a possible settlement.
Earlier in September, the two envoys visited both Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to broker an end to Russia’s war, which reached a deadlock over irreconcilable differences between Ukraine’s and Russia’s demands, including Moscow’s proposals that Kyiv cedes its sovereignty as part of a peace settlement.
Trump Envoys in Talks With Putin’s Money Man Over Russian Gas, Reports Say
Although all three sides – the US, Ukraine and Russia – described the negotiations as productive and positive, the Kremlin consistently rejects proposals for a ceasefire and has increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure since.
Dmitriev, Russia’s envoy who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund and has long pushed for Russian gas exports to Germany to resume, has emerged as one of Moscow’s main points of contact with the Trump administration.
Late September, he headed to New York to meet with the Trump administration, with the agenda previously agreed upon with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Diplomacy remains stalled
Earlier on Thursday, during a visit to Pryluky, where a Russian missile strike killed 22 people the previous day, Zelensky questioned how Washington and Moscow could discuss future economic projects while efforts to end the war remain stalled.
He also announced that a Ukrainian delegation would travel to the US for talks on Friday and Saturday, Oct. 9-10, and called on Trump to increase pressure on Russia.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly argued that Moscow shows no real willingness towards ending the war, pointing to the repeated strikes on Ukrainian cities.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York held late September, 51 countries signed a joint statement urging Russia to accept an immediate, unconditional ceasefire.
However, the Kremlin has rejected and mocked every such proposal so far.
During the same summit in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated that Moscow would not pause its “special military operation” – a term Russia uses to downplay the war in Ukraine, currently in its fifth year – even during negotiations.
He also claimed that Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans.”
The comment came just a month after Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day.

articles.title: Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion
articles.body:
Polish SIM cards were found inside some of the Russian drones that entered Polish airspace during a mass incursion in September 2025, Polish outlet RMF24 reported, citing findings from a Polish prosecution investigation.
SIM cards can allow drones to connect to local cellular networks for functions such as communications, data transmission, telemetry, or navigation-related services. However, investigators have not said what the Polish SIM cards found in the Russian drones were used for. The details remain classified.
The SIM cards were discovered in some of the Russian Gerbera drones recovered after the incursion, RMF24 reported.
Investigators have not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
The investigation into the September 9–10, 2025 incursion was ultimately closed after prosecutors failed to identify those responsible for violating Polish airspace.
More than 30 drones entered Poland
The incursion took place overnight on September 9–10, 2025, during a large Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. More than 30 Russian Gerbera drones entered Polish airspace from the east and came down at 27 locations across the country, according to RMF24.
Polish forces intercepted and shot down multiple drones, with the Territorial Defense Forces deployed to search for wreckage and other objects that came down on Polish territory. Poland also maintained contact with NATO command throughout the operation.
The incident prompted Poland to close four airports – Warsaw Chopin, Warsaw-Modlin, Rzeszów-Jasionka and Lublin – because of the military activity.
Polish officials described the airspace violations as unprecedented and a serious threat to national security. The incident marked the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine that Polish forces had used weapons against Russian aerial objects that entered the country's airspace.
The mass incursion subsequently became the subject of a criminal investigation into the violation of Polish airspace and the threat to public safety.
Investigation closed without identifying perpetrators
After months of investigation, Polish prosecutors closed the case because they were unable to identify the perpetrators, according to Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office spokesman Marcin Kozak, as cited by RMF24.
Most of the case files, including the justification for the decision, are classified.
Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
Prosecutors cleared Poland's military response
Investigators also examined whether the Polish military had responded properly to the drone incursion.
According to RMF24, prosecutors concluded that the military acted in accordance with procedures. Polish troops had the right to use force and shoot down hostile objects, and prosecutors found no irregularities in their response.
The investigation was therefore closed both over the failure to identify the perpetrators and over the assessment of the Polish military's actions.

articles.title: AI is changing Russia’s drone war on Ukrainian cities, deputy air defense commander says
articles.body:
Russian forces appear to use AI to plan air attacks and recognize targets amid raids on Ukrainian cities. This may include recent air attacks on Odesa that have come in waves with short gaps, Deputy Air Force Commander for Air Defense Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko says, Ukrinform reports.
Russia has already equipped its jet-powered Geran-4 drones with machine vision, allowing them to recognize and track targets on their own in the final seconds of flight. Recently, a single jet drone hit a locomotive in Odesa Oblast in late September and killed two railway workers.
The scale of Russia's AI use is hard to measure, Cherevashenko continues, but Ukrainian specialists already see its elements in how attacks are organized. The long, wave-by-wave strikes on Odesa would be far harder to plan and coordinate without it, he believes.
"Russian forces use AI to lay out attack routes and to recognize targets," Cherevashenko says, framing it as his own assessment rather than a confirmed fact.
The sea is harder to defend than land
Odesa Oblast is home to the biggest port in Ukraine, "Southern". Protecting it is a challenging task as guarding the airspace over water is tougher than over land, Cherevashenko says. Some air defense assets do not perform as well at sea, and in some cases, crews can intercept a target only as it approaches.
Weather adds to the problem, with storms and fog, while the open sea gives Russia more freedom to choose drone routes and launch points. To protect ports and the coast, Ukraine uses drone motherships, platforms that carry other drones aloft to extend their flight time and keep watch over set areas.
Ukraine answers AI with AI
Ukraine is also building its own AI for air defense. Automated turrets using machine vision now help counter Russian drones. According to Army Media, the Air Force says such turrets have scored their first shoot-downs, including of Geran-5 jet drones, with one soldier saying 50 rounds were enough to bring down a Geran.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry is going further. In late September, it unveiled an AI system called SPECTR, built by its A1 Artificial Intelligence Center and already in testing with several combat units, to analyze battlefield data, predict Russian moves, and suggest options to commanders.

articles.title: Russia steps up sabotage campaign against Danish companies supplying Ukraine, intelligence service says
articles.body:
Russia has begun organizing sabotage operations against Danish companies that supply goods to Ukraine, Reuters reports, citing Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) senior analyst Josephine Christensen.
Speaking Oct. 7 at a domestic security conference in Copenhagen, Christensen said:
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
The shift marks a significant escalation in Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign, Christensen said, explaining that Russian authorities had concluded that their earlier tactic of targeting a broad range of sites “did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine.” Moscow is now “trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line…that means weapons production,” she said.
According to PET, Russian operatives recruit people through Telegram and social media, first assigning them simple tasks such as gathering information and taking photographs before progressing to involve them in sabotage. The recruits can be random individuals, including homeless people and people with drug addictions.
“It could be anyone just looking for quick money. If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed.”
Politico previously reported that the European Union is discussing possible responses to a hypothetical large-scale hybrid attack by Russia. Those talks intensified after a drone equipped with a detonator was found in early August near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany. Poland has also reported arson attacks and other acts of sabotage that the authorities suspect may be linked to Russia, as has Slovakia.
PET chief Emil Gresholm had previously said that Russian intelligence services were recruiting Danish citizens to carry out acts of sabotage against local defense companies involved in military aid to Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike oil refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones strike oil refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan
Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat, one of Russia’s largest oil refining complexes, in Salavat, Bashkortostan, overnight on October 8, the Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported.
Astra, an independent Telegram channel, reviewed photos and videos from eyewitnesses and concluded that the fire likely broke out on the grounds of Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat. Ukrainian drones have targeted the refinery more than once during the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine.
Bashkortostan authorities declared an air raid alert overnight because of the threat of a Ukrainian drone attack. They have not reported on the aftermath of the attack.
In addition, “drone debris” fell on the grounds of a facility in Krasnodar, according to a local emergency response headquarters. Fragments of the drone damaged a building and sparked a fire. No one was injured, and the facility’s nature was not specified.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses shot down 399 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea since the evening of October 7.
Drone strikes have forced Russian oil refineries to suspend or halt operations, contributing to a fuel crisis in Russia over the summer.
In early October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky promised that Ukraine would step up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia’s Defense Ministry threatened to respond by expanding its strikes on targets in Ukraine.

Ukraine preparing response to new wave of Russian escalation – Zelensky

“Third, we continue to fulfill the requests raised by combat corps and brigade commanders during meetings on the front lines,” the President said.

articles.title: Air defense downs 126 of 142 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
Overnight into October 8, Russian occupation forces attacked Ukraine with 142 strike UAVs, including Shahed drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 126 enemy Shahed, Gerbera, and other types of UAVs," the General Staff's Telegram channel statement reads.
In addition, Russian air attack impacts were recorded at 7 locations, while fallen debris was registered at 4 locations.

articles.title: Zelenskyy responds to Rubio: You cannot negotiate with Russia and talk about a diplomatic stalemate at the same time
articles.body:
Zelenskyy responds to Rubio: You cannot negotiate with Russia and talk about a diplomatic stalemate at the same time
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statement that the war cannot be ended diplomatically because the situation has reached a "stalemate", and called on the US to help Ukraine gain air superiority and increase pressure on Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists in Pryluky, where a Russian missile struck an apartment block on 7 October, killing 22 people, including five children
Quote: "We have heard about many different moments during the war. Many hopeless situations, difficult corners and so on. We – people, leaders, politicians – drive ourselves into a corner… Even on the first day of the war, we were not in a corner. Because one person tried to drive an entire nation into a corner, and the nation rose up and defended its state." [Zelenskyy's references to a "corner" are a wordplay on the Ukrainian translation of Rubio's "stalemate" as "глухий кут" ("dead end"), which contains the word "кут" ("corner") – ed.]
Details: Zelenskyy added that getting out of the corner is not difficult and that this requires increasing economic pressure on Russia, giving Ukraine access to Starlink over Russian territory and not negotiating with Russia on future projects.
"You see, you cannot negotiate economic projects for the future with the Russians on the one hand and, on the other, say that we are at a… diplomatic deadlock. We are not at a diplomatic stalemate. Shut down their entire economy. Shut Russia's mouth. Do not feed them with your sales. Just impose sanctions on their weapons. Open Starlink to us, to Ukraine," the president said.
He recalled that the US had already done this when it attacked Iran, when "Israel had complete control of the skies over Iran".
Quote: "So that means that when you need it, it works like that… Just control the skies to protect yourself. The US has this capability. For them, it costs nothing to help Ukraine. And I said frankly: 'Give it to us, help us protect our skies and dominate the skies. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table. Why? Because he will lose everything. Three, two months – he will lose everything.' And we are waiting for the Chinese to develop this equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where is the truth, where is the honesty? What corner? This is called unwillingness."
Background: Rubio earlier said that ending the Russia-Ukraine war through diplomatic negotiations is currently "proving elusive" because the war has reached a "strategic stalemate". He acknowledged that diplomatic efforts are failing because Russia is demanding full control of the Donbas and Ukraine refuses to accept it.

articles.title: Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
The Saudi civil defence agency said a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh were damaged by debris from a missile interception on Thursday, as Yemen's Houthis announced attacks targeting the capital's airport.
Two witnesses said that a plane at the airport belonging to national flag carrier Saudia had cracks and holes in its fuselage. A source briefed on the matter said three planes suffered damage.
Saudi Arabia leads a pro-government coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen's civil war. The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted Riyadh since the conflict roared back to life in July, vowing to hit critical infrastructure and disrupt Saudi airspace.
The scale and frequency of the attacks on the Saudi capital have been unprecedented in the eight months of wider war in the Middle East.
The Houthis announced three attacks on Thursday against Riyadh airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
Recent attacks have also targeted oil infrastructure in the world's largest crude exporter.
The Houthis on Thursday warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards Riyadh.
The kingdom's civil defence agency said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city. It did not say if there were casualties or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Shelter in place
After resuming their fight against Yemen's internationally recognised government following a four-year lull, the Houthis last month seized all of the country's Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive.
The group, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014. Riyadh's military coalition intervened in 2015 to support the government.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to roll back the Houthis' advance, despite an ambitious counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around a crucial sea route for global energy flows.
In Riyadh, diplomats were instructed to shelter at their respective embassies, some of them told AFP, after explosions echoed around the city on Thursday morning.
There were no text alerts warning residents, as there had been in the past.
An interior ministry campaign has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators of legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
"My daughter called me," one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was "completely distraught".
Two people working in Riyadh's business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
'Heightened vigilance'
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted for passengers.
The airport did not immediately acknowledge disruption, pointing only in a short statement to the "necessity" of contacting airlines before travelling.
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" following the attacks at the airport, which US government employees now need "special authorisation" to use.
Previous attacks killed a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport, as well as an Egyptian and an Algerian national at Abha airport, civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
A humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
After declaring its counter-offensive, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The rival claims have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
The Houthis recently seized areas south of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, cutting it off from the government's temporary capital in Aden and sparking shortages and soaring prices for food and energy.
(AFP)

articles.title: New Russian Drone Wave Targets Kyiv and Western Ukraine After Deadly Strikes on Putin’s Birthday
articles.body:
Russian forces sent another wave of jet-powered attack drones toward Kyiv and several Ukrainian regions in the early hours of Thursday, Oct. 8, triggering fresh air raid alerts just hours after deadly Russian strikes killed 28 people across Ukraine, including five children.
Ukraine’s Air Force warned at approximately 12:55 a.m. that Russian jet-powered drones were approaching Kyiv, including the capital’s northeastern Troieshchyna neighborhood.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Additional Russian drones were tracked toward Brovary, Vasylkiv and Fastiv in Kyiv region, while other threats emerged across northern and western Ukraine.
Kyiv’s Military Administration issued repeated air raid warnings as the drone threat continued overnight. The administration reported an all-clear at approximately 1:24 a.m. Thursday.
Russian drones threaten Lutsk and northern Ukraine
The overnight drone threat extended far beyond the Ukrainian capital.
In western Ukraine, the Air Force warned that a Russian jet-powered drone was approaching Lutsk in Volyn region before reporting that it was directly over the city.
Volyn regional authorities also issued an air raid warning for Lutsk district shortly after midnight as the threat developed.
Further drones were reported heading toward Ovruch in Zhytomyr region and Desna in Chernihiv region, while another was tracked through the Chornobyl exclusion zone toward Zhytomyr region.
Russian drone movements were also reported in the direction of Rivne region.
Bipartisan US Senators Press Trump Administration to Crack Down on Russia’s Shadow Fleet Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
Meanwhile, Russian tactical aviation threatened Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas with guided aerial bombs, prompting additional Air Force warnings.
The alerts indicated continuing Russian aerial activity across multiple regions, although Ukrainian authorities had not confirmed new impacts or casualties linked specifically to Thursday’s early-hours drone wave.
Five children among 28 killed in Wednesday’s attacks
The latest threats came just hours after Russia carried out deadly missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported that 28 people were killed nationwide, including five children.
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a residential apartment building, killing 20 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.
The strike destroyed part of the building, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage for survivors.
In Kyiv, Russian attacks also killed two people and injured residents, including children, as drones struck apartment buildings and sparked fires in residential neighborhoods.
In Desnianskyi district, four people, including two children, were injured when a drone struck a 12-story residential building. Emergency crews rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
In Solomianskyi district, another drone attack set a five-story apartment building ablaze, injuring eight residents.
The renewed drone threats in the early hours of Thursday followed a devastating day of Russian strikes that destroyed Ukrainian homes and killed entire families.
The attacks unfolded on Oct. 7 – Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – leaving 28 Ukrainians dead, including five children.

Ukraine’s Air Force warned at approximately 12:55 a.m. that Russian jet-powered drones were approaching Kyiv, including the capital’s northeastern Troieshchyna neighborhood.
