Additional Russian drones were tracked toward Brovary, Vasylkiv and Fastiv in Kyiv region, while other threats emerged across northern and western Ukraine.
Kyiv’s Military Administration issued repeated air raid warnings as the drone threat continued overnight. The administration reported an all-clear at approximately 1:24 a.m. Thursday.
Russian drones threaten Lutsk and northern Ukraine
The overnight drone threat extended far beyond the Ukrainian capital.
In western Ukraine, the Air Force warned that a Russian jet-powered drone was approaching Lutsk in Volyn region before reporting that it was directly over the city.
Volyn regional authorities also issued an air raid warning for Lutsk district shortly after midnight as the threat developed.
Further drones were reported heading toward Ovruch in Zhytomyr region and Desna in Chernihiv region, while another was tracked through the Chornobyl exclusion zone toward Zhytomyr region.
Russian drone movements were also reported in the direction of Rivne region.

Meanwhile, Russian tactical aviation threatened Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas with guided aerial bombs, prompting additional Air Force warnings.
The alerts indicated continuing Russian aerial activity across multiple regions, although Ukrainian authorities had not confirmed new impacts or casualties linked specifically to Thursday’s early-hours drone wave.

The latest threats came just hours after Russia carried out deadly missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported that 28 people were killed nationwide, including five children.
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a residential apartment building, killing 20 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.
The strike destroyed part of the building, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage for survivors.
In Kyiv, Russian attacks also killed two people and injured residents, including children, as drones struck apartment buildings and sparked fires in residential neighborhoods.
In Desnianskyi district, four people, including two children, were injured when a drone struck a 12-story residential building. Emergency crews rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
In Solomianskyi district, another drone attack set a five-story apartment building ablaze, injuring eight residents.
The renewed drone threats in the early hours of Thursday followed a devastating day of Russian strikes that destroyed Ukrainian homes and killed entire families.
The attacks unfolded on Oct. 7 – Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – leaving 28 Ukrainians dead, including five children.

In western Ukraine, the Air Force warned that a Russian jet-powered drone was approaching Lutsk in Volyn region before reporting that it was directly over the city.
Volyn regional authorities also issued an air raid warning for Lutsk district shortly after midnight as the threat developed.
Further drones were reported heading toward Ovruch in Zhytomyr region and Desna in Chernihiv region, while another was tracked through the Chornobyl exclusion zone toward Zhytomyr region.
Russian drone movements were also reported in the direction of Rivne region.
Bipartisan US Senators Press Trump Administration to Crack Down on Russia’s Shadow Fleet Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
Meanwhile, Russian tactical aviation threatened Zaporizhzhia and surrounding areas with guided aerial bombs, prompting additional Air Force warnings.
The alerts indicated continuing Russian aerial activity across multiple regions, although Ukrainian authorities had not confirmed new impacts or casualties linked specifically to Thursday’s early-hours drone wave.
Five children among 28 killed in Wednesday’s attacks
The latest threats came just hours after Russia carried out deadly missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi reported that 28 people were killed nationwide, including five children.
The deadliest attack struck Pryluky in Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile hit a residential apartment building, killing 20 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.
The strike destroyed part of the building, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage for survivors.
In Kyiv, Russian attacks also killed two people and injured residents, including children, as drones struck apartment buildings and sparked fires in residential neighborhoods.
In Desnianskyi district, four people, including two children, were injured when a drone struck a 12-story residential building. Emergency crews rescued 22 residents, eight of them children.
In Solomianskyi district, another drone attack set a five-story apartment building ablaze, injuring eight residents.
The renewed drone threats in the early hours of Thursday followed a devastating day of Russian strikes that destroyed Ukrainian homes and killed entire families.
The attacks unfolded on Oct. 7 – Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – leaving 28 Ukrainians dead, including five children.

articles.title: Ukrainian strikes blast Russian frigates at Novorossiysk
articles.body:
A single Ukrainian drone attack on Novorossiysk has significantly degraded the land-attack cruise missile capability of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, accounting for forty per cent of its Kalibr-capable surface ships, according to a Defence Intelligence update published by the UK Ministry of Defence.
In its update on Thursday, Defence Intelligence said: “Ukraine has launched two large scale uncrewed aerial system (UAS) attacks against the Russian Novorossiysk Naval Facility and Commercial Port within the last two months. The 08-09 September 2026 attack led to successful strikes against a GRIGOROVICH class frigate and a SVIYAZHSK light-frigate.”
It went on: “Both vessels have likely sustained sufficient damage to prevent them taking part in KALIBR Land-attack Cruise Missile (LACM) firings into Ukraine, likely for the short-medium term. This single attack has significantly degraded the LACM strike capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet, representing 40% of the KALIBR-capable surface fleet.”
Two ships out of action amounting to two fifths of the capability says as much about the size of the remaining fleet as it does about the damage. Russia has been firing Kalibr missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Black Sea platforms since the opening days of the full-scale invasion, and the surface ships able to carry them have never been numerous.
The Admiral Grigorovich class are Project 11356R frigates, the newest conventional surface combatants the Black Sea Fleet has, each able to carry Kalibr in a vertical launch system. Defence Intelligence describes the second vessel as a Sviyazhsk light-frigate, a smaller Kalibr-armed surface combatant.
Ukrainian strikes drove Russian warships out of Sevastopol over the course of 2023 and 2024, and the Krasnodar Krai port became the main operating base for what remained. Pushing the fleet east was supposed to put it beyond easy reach.
Defence Intelligence uses a probability yardstick in which “likely” sits between 55 and 75 per cent, so the assessment that both ships cannot take part in Kalibr firings is a confident judgement without being a certainty. The phrase short to medium term carries no fixed definition, though repairs to a vertical launch system and the surrounding structure on a frigate are not quick work, particularly in a yard under periodic attack.
UK Defence Intelligence publishes its guidance on the use of probabilistic language at this link.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone pilot calls it his proudest strike: cheap FPV drone detonating over two tons of explosives packed inside Russian mine-clearer
articles.body:
"Skipper", an FPV company commander in Ukraine's 413th Raid Unmanned Systems Regiment, has described destroying a Russian UR-77 mine-clearing vehicle with drones during the 2023 counteroffensive as the strike he is proudest of, according to Army TV.
The UR-77, nicknamed "Zmiy Horynych" after a fire-breathing serpent of Slavic folklore, carries a rocket-fired line charge to blow paths through minefields, as per Militarnyi. Each charge carries more than two tons of explosives, which is why a cheap FPV hit can trigger a blast far larger than the drone itself.
"It exploded so hard that I thought it was a small nuclear blast. There are more than two tons of plastic explosive inside, and when it went off after the second hit, it was something unbelievable," Skipper says.
Skipper joined the army at the start of the full-scale invasion and moved from infantry and aerial reconnaissance to commanding an FPV unit. His regiment now operates on the Zaporizhzhia front, where FPV drones conduct combat missions.
From sailing yachts to FPV drones
In civilian life, Skipper was a sailing instructor, and he says the sport partly helps in military work, especially his knowledge of navigation and radio communication. He is convinced that a technological edge can be one of the keys to victory.
He counts the UR-77 strike among his unit's early work, from a time when few Ukrainian units were using FPV drones at all, he says. The hit came during hard fighting in the counteroffensive, when his crews were among the first to work the FPV niche.
Russia turns a mine-clearer into a wrecking tool
The UR-77 was built in the 1970s for a different war, one of fast tank thrusts that needed enemy minefields cleared quickly. Its base rides on the chassis of the 2S1 Gvozdika self-propelled howitzer, and its charge can cut a lane six meters wide, with some anti-personnel mines detonated across a band up to 15 meters wide.
Modern combat changed that role. The classic mine-clearing use remains, but Russia now more often turns these machines on Ukrainian fortifications, using the line charge to flatten defenses rather than open a path.

articles.title: NATO says 'Steadfast Noon' in Italy is a nuclear exercise
articles.body:
NATO on Thursday said its upcoming
'Steadfast Noon' exercise in Italy was a nuclear exercise,
obviously not featuring live weapons.
                                    
The exercise starting in Italy October 13 will be a "nuclear"
exercise, explained NATO's head of nuclear policy, Nassima
Barrows, during a meeting with media outlets, including ANSA.
                                    
While no live nuclear weapons are used in the exercise, training
to the high standards required for a mission of this type
remains crucial.
                                    
"It is therefore essential to ensure both discipline and the
ability to collaborate on collective defense—of which the
nuclear mission is a vital component," stated Colonel David
Bull, the Alliance's Head of Nuclear Operations.
